title: Sinusoidal encoding extrapolation to longer sequences not guaranteed
description: The authors chose sinusoidal positional encodings because they 'may' allow extrapolation to sequence lengths longer than those encountered during training, indicating this ability is uncertain and not empirically verified.
canonical_description: sinusoidal positional encoding extrapolation to unseen sequence lengths not guaranteed

verdict.reasoning: Paper 1 (Dissecting Transformer Length Extrapolation) directly resolves the gap: it empirically verifies that vanilla sinusoidal positional encodings fail to extrapolate beyond training length, diagnoses the root cause (overfitting to training-length positions via cumulative gradient analysis), and proposes Sandwich — a modification that converts sinusoidal encodings into a relative positional embedding that does extrapolate up to 16× training length. This turns the original uncertainty into a concrete answer: sinusoidal encodings are not guaranteed to extrapolate and indeed fail, but a principled modification can fix them. Papers 2, 3, and 4 provide converging partial support (confirming failure via different angles — ExPE treats it as known, RFS gives a theoretical rank-explanation, and the Theoretical Analysis shows periodic ambiguity causes degradation), reinforcing the evidence. Paper 5 (KERPLE) is not relevant. The gap's core question — whether sinusoidal encoding extrapolation is guaranteed/verified — is now resolved with empirical and theoretical grounding, leaving only secondary limitations (e.g., recency bias in Sandwich for non-language tasks) that do not affect the main finding.

paper.title: Dissecting Transformer Length Extrapolation via the Lens of Receptive Field Analysis
paper.abstract: Length extrapolation permits training a transformer language model on short sequences that preserves perplexities when tested on substantially longer sequences. A relative positional embedding design, ALiBi, has had the widest usage to date. We dissect ALiBi via the lens of receptive field analysis empowered by a novel cumulative normalized gradient tool. The concept of receptive field further allows us to modify the vanilla Sinusoidal positional embedding to create ~\textbf{Sandwich}, the first parameter-free relative positional embedding design that truly length information uses longer than the training sequence. Sandwich shares with KERPLE and T5 the same logarithmic decaying temporal bias pattern with learnable relative positional embeddings; these elucidate future extrapolatable positional embedding design.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper directly addresses the uncertainty about sinusoidal positional encoding extrapolation. It first diagnoses why vanilla Sinusoidal fails at length extrapolation: the cumulative normalized gradient analysis shows Sinusoidal overfits to the training sequence length (e.g., focusing on the 512-th token when L_tr=512). The paper then proposes Sandwich, a modification that converts Sinusoidal into a relative positional embedding by keeping only the decay-with-distance biases (inner product of sinusoidal embeddings), which is shown empirically to extrapolate to longer sequences (up to 8192 tokens when trained on 512) across multiple datasets (ArXiv, GitHub, OpenWebText2).
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper fully addresses the gap for the specific case of language modeling with causal attention. It shows that vanilla Sinusoidal does NOT extrapolate, explains why (overfitting to training length positions), and provides a modified version (Sandwich) that does extrapolate. The gap's core question — whether sinusoidal encodings can extrapolate — is answered: vanilla sinusoidal cannot, but a modified version (converted to RPE form) can. The paper also notes limitations: Sandwich still has recency bias that may be problematic for tasks like parity prediction where all tokens are equally important.
evidence_snippets: Sinusoidal can be fixed by dropping the intermediate terms and keeping only the decay-with-distance biases; this leads to the creation of~\textbf{Sandwich}, the first parameter-free relative positional embedding that truly length information uses longer than the training sequence.

To predict the last token (2048-th), Sinusoidal focuses on the 512-th token when $L_{tr}=512$ and the 128-th token when $L_{tr}=128$ as indicated by the sudden jump on their normalized gradient plots. This is because the model has only seen at most $L_{tr}$ positional embeddings and overfitted on them
Sandwich is the first parameter-free RPE that truly makes use of distant token information beyond $L_{tr}=512$. To see this, notice that lower (better) perplexities occur at $L_{ex}>L_{tr}=512$.

paper.title: ExPe: Exact Positional Encodings for Generative Transformer Models with Extrapolating Capabilities
paper.abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to position embeddings in transformer models, named "Exact Positional Embeddings" (ExPE). An absolute positional embedding method that can extrapolate to sequences of lengths longer than the ones it was trained on. Traditional transformer models rely on absolute or relative position embeddings to incorporate positional information into token embeddings, which often struggle with extrapolation to sequences longer than those seen during training. Our proposed method utilizes a novel embedding strategy that encodes exact positional information by overriding specific dimensions of the embedding vectors, thereby enabling a more precise representation of token positions. The proposed approach not only maintains the integrity of the original embeddings but also enhances the model's ability to generalize to more extended sequences. In causal language modeling, our ExPE embeddings significantly reduce perplexity compared to rotary and sinusoidal embeddings, when tested on sequences longer than those used in training.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes ExPE (Exact Positional Embeddings), a novel absolute positional encoding method that overrides specific dimensions of embedding vectors with linearly increasing position values. The paper empirically demonstrates that ExPE can extrapolate to sequences 2x and 4x longer than training length, and compares against sinusoidal and rotary embeddings. In doing so, it provides experimental evidence that sinusoidal positional encodings indeed fail to extrapolate to longer sequences (confirming the gap's uncertainty), while offering ExPE as a solution that does achieve extrapolation.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper does not systematically analyze *why* sinusoidal encodings fail to extrapolate, nor does it verify under what conditions (e.g., different model sizes, training lengths, or data distributions) sinusoidal encodings might or might not extrapolate. The gap is about the *uncertainty* of sinusoidal encoding extrapolation being unverified; this paper treats that failure as a known fact and moves on to propose a new method. A direct solution to the gap would be a rigorous empirical study characterizing when and why sinusoidal encodings do/don't extrapolate. Instead, this paper provides a new method that sidesteps the issue.
evidence_snippets: While this method didn't add any new parameters to the model, it still suffered from the model's inability to extrapolate to sequences longer than those seen during training.

The experiments with this approach yielded a good result ... compared to RoPE, and the model's cross-entropy also remained stable when given inputs that were 2 or 4 times longer than the training data text, which was 512 tokens in length. This is something that relative, rotary, and sinusoidal positional encoding don't achieve.

Our proposed method utilizes a novel embedding strategy that encodes exact positional information by overriding specific dimensions of the embedding vectors, thereby enabling a more precise representation of token positions.

paper.title: Position Encoding with Random Float Sampling Enhances Length Generalization of Transformers
paper.abstract: Length generalization is the ability of language models to maintain performance on inputs longer than those seen during pretraining. In this work, we introduce a simple yet powerful position encoding (PE) strategy, Random Float Sampling (RFS), that generalizes well to lengths unseen during pretraining or fine-tuning. In particular, instead of selecting position indices from a predefined discrete set, RFS uses randomly sampled continuous values, thereby avoiding out-of-distribution (OOD) issues on unseen lengths by exposing the model to diverse indices during training. Since assigning indices to tokens is a common and fundamental procedure in widely used PEs, the advantage of RFS can easily be incorporated into, for instance, the absolute sinusoidal encoding, RoPE, and ALiBi. Experiments corroborate its effectiveness by showing that RFS results in superior performance in length generalization tasks as well as zero-shot commonsense reasoning benchmarks.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper introduces Random Float Sampling (RFS), a position indexing strategy that replaces discrete integer indices with randomly sampled continuous values from [0,1). When applied to sinusoidal positional encodings, RFS allows the model to handle unseen sequence lengths by ensuring the index range is shared between training and inference. The paper also provides a theoretical explanation (in the appendix) for why standard sinusoidal encoding with simple integer extrapolation fails: the rank of the position matrix increases with longer sequences, interfering with the semantic subspace learned during training.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper does NOT empirically verify whether standard sinusoidal positional encodings (with discrete integer indices, unmodified) can extrapolate to longer sequences. Instead, it proposes a modification (RFS) that changes the indexing scheme entirely. The original gap — that sinusoidal encoding extrapolation is "not guaranteed" and uncertain — remains unverified empirically for the standard formulation. The paper's theoretical explanation (rank increase) supports why it's not guaranteed, but does not provide empirical evidence one way or the other for the original unmodified sinusoidal encoding.
evidence_snippets: We argue that the simple extension fails because the rank of the position matrix increases as the input sequence gets longer, interfering with the subspace purely for the semantic information during training.

In this paper, we introduce a novel position indexing approach, Random Float Sampling (RFS), that technically allows the model to work on any input length by strategically selecting position indices from a shared continuous range during training and inference.

The authors chose sinusoidal positional encodings because they 'may' allow extrapolation to sequence lengths longer than those encountered during training, indicating this ability is uncertain and not empirically verified.

paper.title: Theoretical Analysis of Positional Encodings in Transformer Models: Impact on Expressiveness and Generalization
paper.abstract: Positional encodings are a core part of transformer-based models, enabling processing of sequential data without recurrence. This paper presents a theoretical framework to analyze how various positional encoding methods, including sinusoidal, learned, relative, and bias-based methods like Attention with Linear Biases (ALiBi), impact a transformer's expressiveness, generalization ability, and extrapolation to longer sequences. Expressiveness is defined via function approximation, generalization bounds are established using Rademacher complexity, and new encoding methods based on orthogonal functions, such as wavelets and Legendre polynomials, are proposed. The extrapolation capacity of existing and proposed encodings is analyzed, extending ALiBi's biasing approach to a unified theoretical context. Experimental evaluation on synthetic sequence-to-sequence tasks shows that orthogonal transform-based encodings outperform traditional sinusoidal encodings in generalization and extrapolation. This work addresses a critical gap in transformer theory, providing insights for design choices in natural language processing, computer vision, and other transformer applications.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper provides a theoretical analysis of why sinusoidal positional encodings fail to extrapolate to longer sequences, attributing it to periodic repetition causing positional ambiguity. It derives formal extrapolation bounds and empirically demonstrates on a synthetic running-sum task that sinusoidal encodings degrade substantially (MSE 0.0423 at 4× training length) compared to alternatives like wavelet-based encodings (MSE 0.0108). The paper also proposes novel encoding schemes (wavelet, Legendre) that address the extrapolation limitation.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper does not solve the gap in the sense of making sinusoidal encoding extrapolation guaranteed or empirically verified as reliable. Instead, it confirms the uncertainty by showing theoretically and empirically that sinusoidal encodings extrapolate poorly. The gap's core problem — that sinusoidal encoding extrapolation is uncertain/unverified — is addressed by explaining why it fails and proposing alternatives, but the gap itself (the lack of guaranteed extrapolation for sinusoidal encodings) remains open; the paper does not propose a fix or modification to sinusoidal encodings that would make them extrapolate reliably.
evidence_snippets: Sinusoidal encodings repeat periodically in each frequency dimension after $2\pi$ in their argument. Specifically, if $pos' = pos + k \cdot 10000^{2i/d_{\mathrm{model}}}$, then $\mathrm{PE}(pos') = \mathrm{PE}(pos)$ in the $(2i)$-th dimension. ... This ambiguity degrades extrapolation, as the model cannot reliably distinguish very long positions.
Sinusoidal encodings degrade rapidly once $pos$ exceeds training range, as cyclic repetition leads to ambiguous positions.
Sinusoidal encodings degrade substantially (0.0423) because of ambiguity in very long positions.

paper.title: KERPLE: Kernelized Relative Positional Embedding for Length Extrapolation
paper.abstract: Relative positional embeddings (RPE) have received considerable attention since RPEs effectively model the relative distance among tokens and enable length extrapolation. We propose KERPLE, a framework that generalizes relative position embedding for extrapolation by kernelizing positional differences. We achieve this goal using conditionally positive definite (CPD) kernels, a class of functions known for generalizing distance metrics. To maintain the inner product interpretation of self-attention, we show that a CPD kernel can be transformed into a PD kernel by adding a constant offset. This offset is implicitly absorbed in the Softmax normalization during self-attention. The diversity of CPD kernels allows us to derive various RPEs that enable length extrapolation in a principled way. Experiments demonstrate that the logarithmic variant achieves excellent extrapolation performance on three large language modeling datasets. Our implementation and pretrained checkpoints are released at https://github.com/chijames/KERPLE.git.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes KERPLE, a framework for relative positional embeddings using conditionally positive definite (CPD) kernels to enable length extrapolation in transformers. It introduces logarithmic and power variants of relative positional biases and shows they outperform existing methods like ALiBi and T5 on language modeling tasks. The paper does not analyze, verify, or address the extrapolation properties of sinusoidal positional encodings.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap concerns whether sinusoidal positional encodings (absolute position embeddings based on sine/cosine functions) can reliably extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than those seen during training. This paper does not address that question at all — it proposes an entirely different class of positional embeddings (relative, kernel-based) rather than studying the extrapolation properties of sinusoidal encodings. The uncertainty about sinusoidal encoding extrapolation remains completely unaddressed.
evidence_snippets: We propose KERPLE, a framework that generalizes relative position embedding for extrapolation by kernelizing positional differences.
We conduct experiments to cover aspects such as input length extrapolation, application on different domains, and comparison with the prior work.

To validate the effectiveness of our method, we compare KERPLE with Sinusoidal [CITE:vaswani2017attention], Rotary [CITE:su2021roformer], T5 [CITE:raffel2019exploring], and ALiBi [CITE:press2022train].
